title: One delivery loop
subtitle: Jira holds the work. The manager coordinates it. Cursor workers do it. Humans decide what ships.
notes: Read left to right, then follow the worker handoff back into Jira. The manager alone admits work into In Progress; workers retain their role-specific outcome transitions.
Monitoring supplies execution facts, not QA verdicts. PR environments are pipeline-owned separate work. Human approval/unblock action wiring is still to be specified.
This is the proposed target. The saved inactive MVP currently has direct Jira-to-Cursor webhooks; adoption would replace that direct dispatch path, not run both paths.

title: Inside the manager
subtitle: Three responsibilities share a small execution record. These are modules, not three separate services.
notes: Admission chooses which ticket may begin. A stage event for In Review or QA goes to Dispatch for the already-admitted ticket. Pausing an Epic must not accidentally stop those finishing-stage launches.
A production dispatcher needs persistent coordination to suppress repeated deliveries. The mechanism is an open implementation choice; no database is selected here.
The observer reads Cursor status and checks for the role handoff. No transcript mirror, AI supervisor, automatic retry or automatic unblock is proposed.

title: Admit only the next eligible ticket
subtitle: Eligibility comes before priority. Epic membership never makes an unready ticket executable.
notes: The active slot covers the whole automated cycle, not merely the implementer process. In Review and QA occupy the same numbered stream.
Ready to Work is the existing new-work eligibility status. Rework Queued is the agreed separate repair path. No new preparation status is proposed.

A required Bug can precede its dependent queued repair. The five-ticket limit applies to new Bugs as well as new Stories. We still need to formalize abnormal repair/cap states without creating a deadlock.
An Epic that is not In Progress admits nothing; its existing cycle may still drain through review and QA. The opt-in label spelling remains undecided.

title: Workers own evidence and handoffs
subtitle: Only the manager moves work into In Progress. Worker skills decide their own evidence-backed outcomes.
notes: Success flow is implementer → In Review, reviewer → QA, QA → Human Review. There is no worker arrow back to In Progress.
Confirmed repairs queue. An implementer can also queue when a known upstream repair prevents completion. An ordinary repair it can complete within its scope remains part of its job.
Workers publish records on Jira and relevant PR comments/evidence before their allowed handoff. Role skills constrain behavior; provider credentials still determine technical access.

title: Small skills, composed for each role
subtitle: The entry point chooses the prescribed sequence. Job skills execute. The role handoff skill updates Jira.
notes: These are instruction responsibilities, not a proposal to spawn an agent per skill. The three worker types remain separate automations.
The central Pigboard bundle is fetched during deterministic environment setup outside the app repo. All required skills are available; entry points explicitly invoke what their role needs.
Implementer context includes the Epic, its ordered workstream and relevant neighboring PRs. That context does not enlarge the assigned Story scope.
QA uses only the prescribed case sequence; API assessment delegates request execution to its named Bruno child, not a duplicate top-level request.

title: Independent streams, shared worker types
subtitle: A numbered label is the capacity boundary. The suffix never selects a different worker automation.
notes: Daniel-1, Maria-1 and Maria-2 are independent sequential streams. A full label belongs to only one active Epic. A person can have several distinct numbered streams.
Different streams reuse that person’s configured implementer, reviewer and QA automation types. They do not create a separate automation for each suffix.
A stream stays occupied while its current ticket is in automated review or QA. Five waiting human reviews stop new admission, including Bugs. No UI here represents live tickets.

title: Repair the stack without interrupting work
subtitle: A has a confirmed defect. B is already running on top of A. C has not started.
notes: This is the accepted human-review rework scenario. Do not pause the active Cursor run or assume it can resume with intact paid context. Let its current cycle finish.
If B cannot complete because A’s known queued defect prevents its cases, B records NOT RUN for prevented checks, queues and ends. A’s repair can then go first.
Stack relationships, findings and exact verification revisions must be available from durable ticket/PR context, not another agent’s memory.
Human merge/retarget activity alone does not trigger automatic stack maintenance. This diagram concerns confirmed repairs and necessary downstream code changes.

title: Pause admission, finish the active cycle
subtitle: A human moves the Epic out of In Progress. That is not a cancellation request.
notes: Epic state gates admission, not every event. Review and QA for the already-active cycle must still be dispatched when their preceding worker hands off.
If a correction is needed, that requires a new admission from Rework Queued, so it waits. Ready B and C wait too. Genuine inability still goes to Blocked.
When the human starts the Epic again, the manager evaluates current state and starts at most one eligible cycle per stream.

title: Observe execution; humans decide recovery
subtitle: Run state answers “is it active?” Worker evidence answers “did the job succeed?”
notes: Status monitoring does not require AI-generated heartbeats or transcript parsing. The API documentation offers run states; reading our exact webhook-triggered runs still needs verification.
We must not confuse provider completion with successful CI, review approval, QA pass or a Jira transition. Workers remain responsible for those outcomes.

Dispatch uses stage-visit identity to distinguish duplicate delivery from legitimate rework. Persistent coordination is proposed, with no chosen storage. Exactly-once provider launches are not claimed.
A rare uncertain launch gets a human-attention outcome, not a complex automatic recovery system. Polling cadence, permissions and implementation location remain open.
